tips.title: You are given the tonic chord and the pulse
tips.body: Before the melody starts you hear the **tonic chord**, then the **pulse**. That is not a warm-up: the chord tells you where home is, so you can hear every note as a distance from it, and the pulse fixes the speed and the beat before a single note arrives. Use both deliberately.

tips.title: Rhythm first, pitch afterwards
tips.body: The paper splits the job for you: part (a) wants only the **rhythm** of one passage, part (b) only the **pitches** of another, with its rhythm printed. Use the first playing for the rhythm gap, as stems with no noteheads if that is quicker, and the later playings for the pitch gap.

tips.title: Every bar has to add up
tips.body: A bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ holds four crotchets, no more and no less. Counting each finished bar takes seconds and catches one of the commonest errors in the question — a missing quaver or a dot left off, which otherwise costs a mark and drags the next bar out of line too.

tips.title: Use the rough manuscript, then copy it
tips.body: The paper gives you blank manuscript for rough work and says the final answer must be on the printed stave. Draft there, fix it, and copy it across once in black ink, or draft on the stave in pencil and ink over it once you are sure, as the examiners' report suggests. Working straight onto the answer stave means crossings-out, and a bar you cannot read is a bar you cannot be given marks for.

tips.title: Tone, tone, semitone: the major scale's shape
tips.body: A major scale climbs **tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone**, so its only half steps are degrees 3 to 4 and 7 to 8. In C major they are the white-key pairs with no black key between them: E to F and B to C.

why.matters: Writing down what you hear is how anything gets from a performance to a page, and the exam tests it directly with the most predictable question on the paper: a printed score of the melody with two gaps, a tonic chord, a pulse, and the melody played four times. In one gap you write only the rhythm, in the other only the pitches, and each is worth five marks, so a perfect rhythm with the pitches guessed still earns half, and a blank is the only truly expensive mistake. The method is an order of work: the rhythm gap first, every bar adding up, then pitch as same, step or leap.

examples.title: Four playings, ten marks, two halves
examples.body: In the 2019 and 2022 papers the melody was played four times and the ten marks were split five for a passage where you write the rhythm and five for a passage where you write the pitches. That decides the order of work. First playing: the rhythm gap, stems with no heads, tapping the pulse. Second: check that every bar adds up, because a short bar pushes everything after it out of line. Third: the pitch gap, each note as the same, a step or a leap from the last. Fourth: read the whole thing back against the music. Half the marks are banked before a single pitch is written.

the pitch gap: same, step or leap

examples.title: The song learned by ear
examples.body: Anyone who has picked out a tune on a piano after hearing it has done dictation without paper: heard that the second note is higher than the first, that the third is the same, that the phrase lands back where it started. Sheet music for a pop song began the same way, with someone listening and writing. The exam only asks for the paper version, and it gives you more than a room does: the key, the metre, the first note, and the melody four times over.

steps.title: What the question gives you
steps.body:
One question in Section A is **musical dictation**, worth **10 marks** in both the 2019 and 2022 papers. It is the most predictable question on the paper, because its shape barely changes.

Here is what you are handed.

- **A printed score** of the melody with the key signature, the time signature and a tempo marking, and most of the notes already written in. Two short passages are left for you, marked with brackets: in part **(a)** you write only the **rhythm**; in part **(b)** the rhythm is printed above the stave and you write only the **pitches**.
- **The tonic chord**, played before the melody starts.
- **The pulse**, played after the chord.
- **The melody, played several times.** The paper prints how many, and the audio announces it.
- **Blank manuscript** for rough work, with the instruction that the final answer must go on the printed stave.

In the 2019 and 2022 papers the melody was played **four times**, and the ten marks were split **five for the rhythm and five for the pitches**. In 2022 each part had five notes to find, one mark per note.

> The two parts are marked separately, and each note on its own. A rhythm that is right with the pitches missing still earns the rhythm marks, and a guessed note can still score.

That changes how you should work. A blank is the only truly expensive mistake, and the rhythm part, which the 2022 examiners' report says candidates found much easier, is worth going after first and hardest.

**The given bars are not decoration.** They tell you the key, the metre and the note the melody starts from. Read them in the reading time, before anything is played.

steps.title: Rhythm first, and why
steps.body:
The rhythm part is the easier half (the 2022 examiners' report says candidates found the rhythmic dictation much easier than the melodic), and it is worth as many marks, so bank it first.

**On the first playing, write only the rhythm gap.** Stems with no noteheads are fine; you can add the heads later.

**Tap the pulse and keep tapping.** Every note is either on a beat or between beats, and that is almost the whole of rhythmic dictation.

**The note values you need.**

| Note | Worth |
| --- | --- |
| semibreve | 4 crotchets |
| minim | 2 crotchets |
| crotchet | 1 beat in $\tfrac{4}{4}$ |
| quaver | half a crotchet |
| semiquaver | a quarter of a crotchet |

**A dot adds half again.** A dotted minim is three crotchets; a dotted crotchet is a crotchet and a quaver; a dotted quaver is a quaver and a semiquaver. One of the commonest rhythms in dictation is a **dotted crotchet followed by a quaver**, which fills two beats.

**Every bar must add up.** In $\tfrac{4}{4}$ a bar holds the equivalent of four crotchets — no more, no less. Counting each bar as you finish it is the single most useful habit in this question, because a bar that is short does not just lose its own mark, it pushes everything after it out of line.

**Watch for a change of time signature.** The 2019 melody moved from four-four to three-four and back, and used triplets, so check each bar against the signature in force for it.

visuals.alt: A table of three time signatures with the amount each bar holds and an example filling for each

check.prompt: A dotted crotchet is worth how much?
check.solution: A dot adds **half again** to the note it follows. Half a crotchet is a quaver, so a dotted crotchet is a crotchet plus a quaver — three quavers in total.

check.prompt: A bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ contains a minim and a crotchet. What is still needed to complete it?
check.solution: A minim is two beats and a crotchet is one, making three. A $\tfrac{4}{4}$ bar holds four, so one more crotchet is needed.

steps.title: Pitch: same, step, or leap
steps.body:
In the pitch part the rhythm is printed above the gap, so you already know how many notes there are and where each falls. The pitches are then a much smaller problem than they look, because you never have to identify a note in the abstract. You only ever have to answer one question about each note:

> Is it the **same** as the one before, a **step** away, or a **leap**?

Most notes in a dictation melody are steps. Steps are next-door notes on the stave — a line to the space above it, or a space to the line above. If it is a step, you do not need to identify anything: just move one place.

**Only the leaps need work**, and there are not many kinds.

| Leap | Sounds like |
| --- | --- |
| third | the first two notes of a common chord; a comfortable hop |
| fourth | the opening of *Away in a Manger*; a firm, open jump |
| fifth | the opening of *Twinkle, Twinkle*; open and hollow |
| octave | the opening of *Somewhere Over the Rainbow*; the same note, higher |

Having a song in your head for each of those is the whole trick. Examiners do not care how you identified it.

**Use the tonic.** The chord played at the start told you where home is. A melody that has wandered often returns to the tonic, and recognising that moment re-anchors everything after it.

**The key signature does the accidentals for you.** In G major the F is already sharp, so you write F with no sharp beside it. Adding one is redundant but does not change the note. The mistake that does change a note is the reverse: a note **outside** the key signature needs its own sign. The 2019 melody, in G major, had a B flat that had to be written as one.

**Two places in a major scale are only a semitone apart**: between the third and fourth degrees, and between the seventh and eighth. Everywhere else is a whole tone. That is why the seventh pulls so strongly up to the tonic, and hearing that pull is often what tells you a phrase has ended.

check.prompt: In a major scale, between which degrees do the two semitones fall?
check.solution: A major scale is tone, tone, **semitone**, tone, tone, tone, **semitone**. The semitones are therefore between the third and fourth degrees and between the seventh and eighth. That second one is why the seventh pulls so strongly up to the tonic.

steps.body: Pitches are worked out as a chain of distances from the last note you are sure of, not as a row of separate notes. The given bar is where the chain starts.

check.solution: Counting inclusively from the tonic — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — a fifth up lands on degree **5**, the dominant.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
You cannot practise the listening here — that needs the real recordings, and past papers are where to find them. What you can do here is everything that surrounds the listening, which is where most of the lost marks are.

**Part A — the question itself.**

1. How many marks was the dictation question worth in the 2019 and 2022 papers?
2. What two things are played before the melody starts, and in that order?
3. Where must your final answer be written, and what is the blank manuscript for?

**Part B — bars that must add up.**

4. A bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ has a dotted crotchet and a quaver so far. How much is left?
5. A bar of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ has a crotchet and a quaver. How much is left?
6. Write down two different ways of filling a bar of $\tfrac{6}{8}$.

**Part C — the ones worth thinking hardest about.**

7. Why is it worth writing the rhythm down even when you cannot hear the pitches at all?
8. A student writes every F with a sharp beside it in a piece in G major. The notes are still right, so what is the accidental mistake that would actually cost a mark?

For question 4, work in beats and remember what the dot adds.

visuals.alt: A blank five-row table with a column for working and a column for the answer

check.prompt: A bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ already contains a dotted crotchet and a quaver. How much is left to fill?
check.solution: A dotted crotchet is one and a half beats and a quaver is half a beat, making two. A $\tfrac{4}{4}$ bar holds four, so **two beats** remain — a minim, or two crotchets, or any other combination worth two.

steps.title: Going deeper: the checks that finish the question
steps.body:
Two students hear the same melody equally well and come out several marks apart, because one of them checks and the other stops writing when the audio stops.

**Check one: does every bar add up?** Run through bar by bar in beats. This is one of the commonest errors in the question and the easiest to find.

**Check two: does the ending make sense?** Whole melodies usually end on the **tonic** or the **dominant**, but a gap can stop on any note: in 2022 the pitches to fill in ended on B, the third of G major. So use the printed note after the gap: if your last note does not lead to it sensibly, a leap was probably misjudged earlier. Work backwards from the end and see whether a different leap makes the whole phrase land better.

**Check three: do the accidentals match the key signature?** In a key with one sharp, every F is sharp without being marked, and writing the sharp again is redundant but harmless. What does cost a mark is a note outside the key signature written without its sign: the 2019 melody, in G major, had a B flat that needed its flat.

**Check four: is anything blank?** Each note in the gaps is marked on its own, so a guessed note can still earn a mark. A blank earns nothing. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so there is never a reason to leave one.

**And a habit worth building now.** When you practise with a past paper, write the rhythm on the first playing and stop — deliberately — even if you think you could get some pitches. Doing it in the right order is a skill, and the exam is not the place to try it for the first time.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Dictation is one question in **Section A**, worth **10 marks** in the 2019 and 2022 papers.
- You are given the key signature, the time signature, a tempo marking and **most of the melody**, with two gaps: one for the **rhythm**, one for the **pitches**.
- The **tonic chord** is played, then the **pulse**, then the melody several times. The number of playings is printed.
- **Rhythm and pitch are marked separately**: five marks each in 2019 and 2022, one mark per note in 2022.
- **First playing: rhythm only.** Tap the pulse and keep tapping.
- A **dot adds half again**. A dotted crotchet is a crotchet plus a quaver.
- **Every bar must add up** to the time signature. Check each one as you finish it.
- For pitch, ask only: **same, step, or leap?** Most notes are steps.
- Identify leaps by a song you know: a fourth, a fifth, an octave.
- A major scale has semitones only between degrees **3 to 4** and **7 to 8**.
- The **key signature supplies its own accidentals**; a note outside it needs its own sign.
- Draft on the **rough manuscript**, then copy onto the printed stave once.
- **Never leave a note blank.** Each one is marked on its own.
- Whole melodies usually end on the **tonic** or the **dominant**, but a gap can stop on any note. Check that your last note leads to the printed one after it.

questions.prompt: In which section of the Appraising paper does the dictation question appear?
questions.skill: reading what the question gives you
questions.solution: Section A holds the eight listening questions, one of which is the dictation. Section B is the single extended comparison question.

questions.prompt: What is played immediately before the dictation melody?
options: The pulse, then the whole melody slowly
A scale in the key of the piece
The tonic chord, then the pulse
questions.skill: reading what the question gives you
questions.solution: The **tonic chord** comes first, fixing where home is, and then the **pulse**, fixing the beat. Both arrive before the melody so you can use them.

markScheme.description: the tonic chord, then the pulse

questions.prompt: How many crotchets does one bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ hold? Give the number.
questions.solution: Four. The lower number says the beat is a crotchet and the upper number says there are four of them.

questions.prompt: A dot after a note does what?
options: Adds half the note value again
questions.solution: A dot **adds half again**. A dotted minim is three crotchets, and a dotted crotchet is a crotchet plus a quaver. The dot above or below a notehead, rather than after it, is the one that means staccato.

questions.prompt: A bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$ contains a dotted crotchet and a quaver. How much is left to fill?
questions.solution: The dotted crotchet is one and a half beats and the quaver is half a beat, making two. Four less two leaves **two beats**.

questions.prompt: How many quavers fill one bar of $\tfrac{6}{8}$?
questions.solution: The lower number says the unit is a quaver and the upper number says there are six of them. Six quavers are usually written as two dotted crotchets, which is what gives $\tfrac{6}{8}$ its lilting, two-in-a-bar feel.

questions.prompt: A melody leaps up from the tonic by a perfect fifth. Which degree of the scale does it land on? Give the number.
questions.solution: Counting inclusively — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — it lands on degree **5**, the dominant, seven semitones above the tonic.

questions.prompt: In a major scale, where do the two semitones fall?
options: There are no semitones in a major scale
questions.solution: The pattern is tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. That puts the semitones between the third and fourth degrees and between the seventh and eighth.

questions.prompt: Why is it sensible to do the rhythm gap on the first playing and leave the pitch gap until later?
options: The rhythm marks are worth more
It is the easier half, so bank it first
Pitches cannot be heard on a first playing
The examiner only marks the first playing
questions.solution: Rhythm is the easier half and it is worth as much: the 2022 examiners' report says candidates found the rhythmic dictation much easier than the melodic. Banking those five marks first leaves the later playings free for the pitch gap, where the rhythm is already printed for you.

questions.prompt: A bar of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ contains one crotchet and one quaver. How many quavers are still needed to complete it? Give the number.
questions.solution: A $\tfrac{3}{4}$ bar holds three crotchets, which is six quavers. A crotchet is two quavers and the quaver is one, making three used, so **three** quavers remain.

questions.skill: reading what the question gives you
questions.solution: Read first, in the reading time, because the given bars supply the key, the metre and the note your ear starts from. Then use the tonic chord and pulse as they are played. Rhythm on the first playing, pitches on the later ones, since the rhythm makes the pitches easier to place. Then check every bar adds up, and only then copy the answer across.

questions.prompt: A student writes every F with a sharp beside it in a piece with one sharp in the key signature. What is wrong with this?
options: Accidentals are not allowed anywhere in a dictation answer
The key signature already sharpens every F
questions.solution: A key signature applies to **every** note of that letter, in every octave, for the whole piece. Writing the sharp again does not change the note, but it is redundant. The case that matters is the reverse: a note outside the key signature needs its own sign, or it reads as the wrong note.

markScheme.description: the key signature already does it

questions.prompt: You have filled in the final bars of a dictation melody, and your version ends on the sixth degree of the major key the tonic chord established. What does this most likely mean?
options: The tonic chord was played in the wrong key
Nothing; it is the usual ending
A leap was misjudged earlier in the phrase
questions.solution: Whole melodies usually end on the **tonic** or the **dominant**, and the tonic chord has already told you the key. Ending on the sixth is possible but unusual, so it is worth working backwards through the phrase and asking whether a leap was heard a step too large or too small.

questions.prompt: In the 2019 and 2022 papers the dictation was worth ten marks in total, split evenly between the missing rhythm and the missing pitches. How many marks were available for the rhythm alone?
questions.skill: reading what the question gives you
questions.solution: The ten marks were split evenly: 5 for the rhythm and 5 for the melody. That split is why a plausible rhythm is worth writing even when the pitches defeat you.

questions.prompt:
A student says: "I could not hear the pitches at all in the dictation, so I left the whole answer blank and spent the time on the next question."

Explain why this was the wrong decision, and describe what they should have done with the playings instead.
questions.solution: The decision was wrong because the dictation question is not marked as a single whole. Part (a) asks only for the rhythm of one passage and part (b) only for the pitches of another — five marks each in the 2019 and 2022 papers, with each note marked on its own — so the pitches being inaudible removes at most half of what was available. A student who writes the rhythm and guesses the pitches can still earn the rhythm marks and perhaps a pitch or two, whereas a blank answer earns nothing at all. There is also no penalty for writing something wrong, so leaving a bar empty can only cost marks and can never save any. What they should have done is this. In the reading time, before anything was played, read the given bars for the key signature, the time signature and the note the melody starts from. When the tonic chord sounded, fix that pitch in the head as home, and when the pulse followed, start tapping it and keep tapping right through the extract. On the first playing, ignore pitch entirely and write only the rhythm, marking where each note falls against the beat being tapped; stems without noteheads are enough at this stage. On the later playings, fill the pitch gap, whose rhythm is printed, working from the last given note and asking of each one only whether it is the same, a step, or a leap. Finally, count every bar in beats against the time signature and correct any that do not add up, then copy the whole thing onto the printed stave from the rough manuscript. Even if half the pitches were still missing at the end, that approach would have secured a good share of the rhythm marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use the tonic chord, the pulse and the given bars in a dictation question, and explain what each one contributes that the others do not.
questions.skill: reading what the question gives you
questions.solution: The three things arrive in a deliberate order and each does something the others cannot. The given bars come first, because they are printed and can be read in the reading time before any audio begins. They supply the key signature, which tells you which sharps or flats apply throughout and therefore which accidentals you will not need to write; the time signature, which tells you exactly how much every bar must hold; and the first note or two, which is the pitch your ear will measure everything else against. None of that requires listening, so none of it should be left until the music starts. The tonic chord is played next. Its job is to fix the sense of home in the ear. Once you know where the tonic is, you no longer have to identify notes in the abstract: each one becomes a distance from a note you already have, and the melody's returns to the tonic become obvious landmarks that re-anchor you if you lose your place. The pulse follows. It fixes the beat and the speed, which the tempo marking only describes in words. I would start tapping it quietly as soon as it sounds and keep tapping right through the extract, because every note is then either on a beat or somewhere between two beats, and that is very nearly the whole of rhythmic dictation. Together they cover the three things you need before writing anything: what the notes are measured from, how fast they are coming, and how much each bar must contain.

The given bars come first, because they are printed and can be read in the reading time before any audio begins. They supply the key signature, which tells you which sharps or flats apply throughout and therefore which accidentals you will not need to write; the time signature, which tells you exactly how much every bar must hold; and the first note or two, which is the pitch your ear will measure everything else against. None of that requires listening, so none of it should be left until the music starts. The tonic chord is played next. Its job is to fix the sense of home in the ear. Once you know where the tonic is, you no longer have to identify notes in the abstract: each one becomes a distance from a note you already have, and the melody's returns to the tonic become obvious landmarks that re-anchor you if you lose your place. The pulse follows. It fixes the beat and the speed, which the tempo marking only describes in words. I would start tapping it quietly as soon as it sounds and keep tapping right through the extract, because every note is then either on a beat or somewhere between two beats, and that is very nearly the whole of rhythmic dictation. Together they cover the three things you need before writing anything: what the notes are measured from, how fast they are coming, and how much each bar must contain.

questions.prompt: What is the blank manuscript on the paper for?
options: Rough work, to be copied onto the printed stave
The final answer, instead of the stave
Nothing; it is a printing error
questions.solution: The paper provides it for **rough work** and states that the final answer must go on the printed stave. Drafting there and copying across once avoids an answer buried under crossings-out, and a bar that cannot be read cannot be given marks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best reason for identifying a leap by thinking of a song you know?
options: Examiners award marks for naming the song
It reliably names the interval, and the method is not marked
It is the only way intervals can be identified
It replaces the need to check the bar lengths
questions.solution: The mark is for the note being in the right place, not for how you got there. A remembered opening — a fourth, a fifth, an octave — gives a reliable reference under exam pressure, which is exactly when abstract interval recognition tends to desert people.

markScheme.description: it works, and the method is not marked

questions.prompt: Write a short guide, for a student sitting this paper next week, on the four checks to make on a completed dictation before moving on. For each check, say what to look for and what a failure usually means.
questions.solution: Four checks, in this order, and none of them takes long. First, go through bar by bar and count the beats. Every bar must match the time signature exactly: in four four that is the equivalent of four crotchets, no more and no less. If a bar comes up short it is almost always a missing quaver or a dot that was heard but not written, and the reason this check matters most is that a short bar does not only lose its own mark, it pushes everything after it out of alignment as well. Second, look at the last note. Whole melodies usually finish on the tonic or the dominant, because that is what makes a phrase sound finished, although a gap can stop on any note, so check that your last note leads sensibly to the printed note after it. If the melody's ending comes out on the sixth or the seventh degree, that is not impossible, but it is unusual enough to be worth checking, and the cause is almost always a leap earlier in the phrase heard a step too wide or too narrow. Work backwards from the end and see whether a different leap makes the whole shape land better. Third, check the accidentals against the key signature. A key signature applies to every note of that letter in every octave for the whole piece, so in a key with one sharp every F is sharp without being marked, and writing the sharp again is redundant but harmless. The real danger is the reverse: a note outside the key signature, such as the B flat in the 2019 melody in G major, must carry its own sign, or it is marked as the wrong note. Fourth, make sure nothing at all is blank. Each note in the gaps is marked on its own, so a guessed note can still earn a mark, while an empty one earns nothing. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so there is never a reason to leave one.

the ending checked against the tonic, dominant or the printed note after the gap
an odd ending means a misjudged leap
accidentals checked against the key signature

examTechnique.body:
**Read the given bars before the music starts.** They carry the key signature, the time signature and the first notes. That is free information and it is there so you can use it.

**The tonic chord fixes home; the pulse fixes the beat.** Both are played before the melody. Tap the pulse quietly and keep tapping through the extract.

**First playing: the rhythm gap.** Do not chase pitches. Mark where the notes fall against the beat you are tapping.

**Second and third playings: the pitch gap.** Its rhythm is printed above it. Work from the last given note. Ask of each note: same, a step, or a leap? Steps are easy; only leaps need identifying, and most are a third, a fourth, a fifth or an octave.

**Count every bar.** In $\tfrac{4}{4}$ each bar must hold the equivalent of four crotchets. A bar that does not add up is wrong even if every pitch in it is right.

**Use the rough manuscript**, then copy your answer onto the printed stave once, in black ink.

**Do not leave notes empty.** Each note in the gaps is marked on its own, so a guess can score and a blank cannot.

**Join each gap to the music around it.** Your last note should lead sensibly into the printed note after the gap, and a whole melody usually ends on the tonic or the dominant. If yours lands somewhere strange, check the last leap again.
examinerErrors: Chasing pitch and rhythm at the same time on the first playing, and getting neither.
Ignoring the tonic chord played before the melody, then having no reference for the pitches.
Writing bars that do not add up to the time signature.
Forgetting the dot, so a dotted crotchet and quaver pair is written as two crotchets.
Leaving the rhythm blank because the pitches were too hard, when the two are marked separately.
Writing the final answer straight onto the printed stave and crossing it out until it cannot be read.
Leaving the final answer in pencil: the examiners' report reminds candidates it must be in black ink.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer uses the tonic chord and the pulse rather than waiting politely through them, and has the rhythm sketched before the first playing ends. It treats pitch as a set of distances from the last note rather than as a row of unrelated notes, so it only has to identify the leaps. It counts every bar against the time signature before moving on, drafts on the rough manuscript and copies across once. And it never leaves a note empty, because each note is marked on its own and a guess can still score.
